title: ACCIDENTAL DEATHS & SUICIDES IN INDIA - 1993 N.C.R.B.- 16 1.3.4 Approximately one-fourth of the total ‘Accidental Deaths’ were reported due to ‘Road Accidents’ during the year, a large majority (91%) of which were due to motor vehicle mishaps. TABLE-3.1 presents the distribution of ‘Motor Vehicles Deaths’ and their rate of occurrence in various States/UTs during the years 1992 & 1993. It is interesting to note that although the number of Motor Vehicles increased by 10.3 per cent in the country during 1992 and by another 7.6 per cent in 1993, the rate of ‘Accidental Deaths’ per thousand ‘Motor Vehicles’ surprisingly decreased by 2.2 and 7.8 per cent respectively during the same period. Contrary to expectations, the highest rate of deaths was reported from hill states of Himachal Pradesh (4.47) and Meghalaya (4.07) which was more than double the National average. The comparatively higher growth in the number of vehicles in the country has, no doubt, contributed to the decline in the above rate of motor vehicle accidents. However other highly correlated factors like growing safety consciousness amongst drivers and pedestrians in obeying traffic regulations, increased electrification and better conditions of the roads, hi-technology checks using computerised periscope vans, radar guns, video traffic monitors etc. coupled with more intensive and extensive monitoring of the vehicular movements by the traffic police are expected to have contributed in the reduction of the accident rate.

section: Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2001
title: Though the children’s population (up to 14 years age) as per census 2001 was 30.4 per cent of the total population, children accounted for 9.4 per cent in the proportion of victims of accidental deaths. In general males, accounting for 72.4 per cent of total victims were at a greater risk from accidents than females. Most of the victims of accidents were aged between 15 to 44 years. This group of people constituted nearly two-third (60.4%) of all persons killed in the accidents in the country. Causes of Accidental Deaths The percentage of ‘Accidental Deaths’ due to Natural Causes and those due to Un-Natural Causes were 13.5% and 86.5% respectively. The total deaths due to Accidents increased by 5.9 per cent over the previous year. However, the magnitude of ‘Accidental Deaths’ by Natural Causes increased by (111.1%) and that of deaths by Un-Natural Causes decreased by 1.7 per cent during 2001. The share of deaths due to Natural causes in total accidental deaths increased to 13.5 per cent compared to 6.8 per cent in the previous year. The share of deaths due to natural calamities such as ‘Earthquake’, ‘Avalanche’, ‘Lightning’ and Un- Natural causes such as ‘Collapse of Structure’, ‘Killing by Animals’, ‘Sudden Deaths’, ‘Mines or Quarry disaster’, ‘Falls’, ‘Poisoning’, ‘Factory/Machine Accidents’, ‘Killing by Fire Arms’ and ‘Rail-Road Accidents’ has increased. The same has decreased due to Natural causes such as ‘Flood’, ‘Starvation/Thirst’, ‘Torrential Rain’, ‘Cold & Exposure’, ‘Cyclone/Tornado’ and Un-Natural causes such as ‘Air Crash’, ‘Stampede’, ‘Explosion’, ‘Fire’, ‘Suffocation’, and ‘Drowning’, etc. The average rate of Accidental Deaths has marginally increased from 25.5 in 2000 to 26.4 in 2001 due to increase of rate for all major causes of Accidental Deaths. title: 36 ## Offences Under Local And Special Laws. 1.7. A total number of 29,84,654 offences were reported under the local and special laws during 1986 against a total of 14,05,835 cognizable cases registered in 1986 under the Indian Penal Code and 30,96,481 cases under the Local and Special Laws registered in 1985. There was thus a decline of 3.6% in the crime under Local and Special Laws over the year 1985 figures. As compared to 1985 the number of cases registered was less under all the crime heads of Local and Special Laws except Prohibition Act, Customs Act and Indian Railways Act. The States which registered highest number of cases under Local and Special Laws was Tamil Nadu (8,19,473) followed by Andhra Pradesh (5,49,723), Maharashtra 5,09,589 Karnataka (3,71,896), Uttar Pradesh (2,29,110), Gujarat (1,68,440) and West Bengal (1,10,500). In India, as a whole the number of cases registered under the Local and Special Laws is more than twice the number of cases registered under the Indian Penal Code.

title: 119 The phenomenon of urban crimes is an important feature in metropolitan cities but the pattern varies from city to city. 2.3.2 India is predominantly a rural country as only 25.7 per cent of its population lives in urban areas (as per 1991 census) while majority of the population(74.3%) lives in rural areas. Of the total Urban population (2,171.8 lakhs), nearly one-third (769.9 lakhs) constituting 35.44 per cent live in 23 metropolitan cities (one million plus population). The proportion of metropolitan cities population to the national population is 8.7 per cent. There is no demarcation between rural and urban areas as far as the crime statistics are concerned since these were not collected on this basis, but as the crimes in urban areas are peculiar and have shown a consistent rise parallel to the population increase, during the previous few decades, it has generated interest to make a study of the crime phenomenon. An attempt has been made to highlight the prevalence of some crimes in the Urban areas. For the sake of analysis of crime situation in these areas we have confined ourselves with the available data of above mentioned 23 Metropolitan Cities only.

title: Property Stolen and Recovered
pdf_title: CHAPTER-12 PROPERTY STOLEN AND RECOVERED Value of Property Stolen & Recovered - National Level 12.1.1 The details of the property stolen and subsequently recovered alongwith the percentage of recovery (year-wise) during the decade 1986-96 have been presented in Table-73. The percentage changes in these attributes over the decade have also been shown in this table. 12.1.2 During the year 1996, property worth Rs. 99,670 lakhs was reported stolen in the country. This loss was lower by 6.2 per cent over the previous year. However, the value of property lost increased by 354.6 per cent during the decade 1986-96. 12.1.3 Property worth Rs. 28,142 lakhs was recovered during 1996 as against property lost (stolen) of Rs. 99,670 lakhs. The value of property recovered showed an addition of 9.4 per cent over the previous year. pdf_title: Chart-8.4 PERCENTAGE DISTRIBUTION OF DACOITY CASES REPORTED DURING 1998 (BY PLACE OF OCCURRENCE) Robbery 8.8.1 Table 41 represents the State, UT and city-wise information on the number of cases reported and the value of property robbed at various `Places of Occurrence' in the country during 1998. 47.6% of the total cases of Robbery were reported at Other Places. 41.1 per cent of the property loss (by value) in the country was also reported at `Other Places'. Out of 1207 cases of Robbery at `Commercial Establishments', Bihar reported 184 such cases with a property loss of Rs. 151.8 lakhs, followed by Maharashtra, 170 cases with a property loss of Rs. 285.5 lakhs. Maharashtra reported the highest number (85) of Robberies at `Railways' which accounted for 21.9 per cent of the total Robberies at Railways. Out of 62 cases of Bank robberies in the country, as many as 21 were reported in Bihar, followed by Uttar Pradesh with 15 cases. Together, these two States accounted for 58.1 per cent of the total cases and 40.9 per cent of the total value lost in Bank robberies reported in the country. The highest incidents of robbery at `Residential Premises' were recorded in the Metropolitan city of Delhi (297) and `Commercial Establishments' at Madurai (76). `Highway' robberies were more in Kanpur (216) and Patna (201). All 13 cases of robberies under `Railways' were reported from Delhi. pdf_title: CHAPTER-15 POLICE CASUALTIES 15.1.1 The very nature of Policeman's job generates animosity, thereby, endangering their own life in discharge of their Official duties. This includes operations against terrorists, extremists, robbers, dacoits or the resultant accidents. At times, police personnel are not able to cope up with the work culture and are, therefore, driven to commit suicide. 15.1.2 The State, UT & City-wise information relating to Police Personnel Killed or injured on duty during various operations and accidents is provided in Table-85, while the rank-wise casualties or injuries sustained by these personnel is given in Table-86 from the current issue additional data on age-groups of Police personnel who died natural deaths or un-natural deaths are also compiled and presented through Tables 85-A & 85-B. 15.1.3 A total number of 2,730 Police Personnel died during the year. 932 were killed while performing their duties, while, 1,652 died natural deaths and 146 committed suicides. Police Personnel killed on duty 15.2.1 The casualties include Civil as well as the Armed Personnel of various States & UTs who sacrificed their lives while performing their bonafide duties during the year. The magnitude of Police fatalities while performing their duties increased by whooping 47.7 percent as compared to previous year. Of the 932 Police Personnel killed, 908 Personnel belonged to 25 States and 24 Personnel to the 7 Union Territories. 15.2.2 While 53.5 per cent of the casualties occurred due to `Accidents', 19.0 per cent were killed by criminals. 'Anti- Terrorist/Extremists' operations claimed 21.5 percent while `Anti-Dacoity' Operations accounted for 2.8 per cent of the Police casualties. 15.2.3 Jammu & Kashmir suffered the highest casualties (104) followed by Uttar Pradesh (95), and Punjab (85). The N.C.T. of Delhi reported 19 deaths out of a total of 24 reported from the 7 Union Territories. From the State of Sikkim, the Union Territory of A & N Island, Daman & Diu, Lakshadweep and Pondicherry, no Policeman was reported killed on duty during the year. PRISON STATISTICS - 1995 From the available data from the 23 States/UTs, it is seen that the total occupancy exceeded the available total jail capacity in the UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Delhi and in the States of Sikkim, Bihar, Jammu & Kashmir, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and Goa. The highest occupancy of inmates during 1995 was recorded in Dadra & Nagar Haveli (326%). This was followed by UT of Delhi (269%) and the States of Sikkim (163%), Bihar (144%), Jammu & Kashmir (137%), Maharashtra (135%), Meghalaya (124%), Orissa (116%), Uttar Pradesh (115%) and Goa (111%). The occupancy in remaining States/UTs was less than the capacity of jails.

title: N.C.R.B., (M.H.A.) PRISON STATISTICS - 2000 A total of 799 prisoners died in jails by natural and unnatural causes during 2000 in the country. Of 799 deaths, 729 were natural whereas 70 deaths were due to unnatural causes. Thus, natural deaths accounted for 91.2 percent of the total deaths. Uttar Pradesh reported highest number of 112 natural deaths during the year. This was followed by Maharashtra (102), Andhra Pradesh (76), Bihar (74), Tamil Nadu (70), Madhya Pradesh (48) and Orissa (45).
